  • 12 Oct 2026

    Cyberattacks on Food Retailers: Ahold Delhaize Takes Some Systems Offline; Danfoss Freezers in French Supermarkets Sabotaged

    In a Monday, October 12 press release, Netherlands-based food retailer Ahold Delhaize confirmed that it took some of its IT systems offline following a cybersecurity incident. While the company said its "stores are open and serving customers," reports from its US Stop & Shop supermarkets indicate that employees are experiencing difficulties accessing schedules and paystubs, and customers have reported they are unable to access websites, apps, and customer service platforms for Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall in the Netherlands and Delhaize in Belgium. In November 2024, Ahold Delhaize experienced a ransomware attack that affected its US network; the attackers stole sensitive personal information belonging to 2.2 million individuals. The company operates more than 9,400 retail food stores in Europe, the US, and Indonesia. Over the weekend, control systems for Danfoss freezers installed in French supermarkets were remotely hijacked. The appliances' thermostat settings were altered, resulting in spoiled food. The incident has affected between 250 and 350 stores, including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour Market, Monoprix, and Leclerc.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 9

      The similarities between this attack and the unexplained refrigeration failures at US military commissaries in August deserve investigation, although I don't believe a connection has been established. What makes the French incident particularly interesting is that attackers used a legitimate defrost function to cause physical and economic damage across hundreds of stores. An important commonality is the compromise of refrigeration controls across multiple locations, producing physical consequences without compromising the stores' primary IT systems. The engineer inside of me would like to know why a remotely issued command is allowed to drive refrigeration equipment into an unsafe operating condition without an independent temperature limit, alarm, or protective mechanism.

      Marcus (Marc) SachsSenior Vice President and Chief Engineer
    • Slide 2 of 9

      We've spent a lot of time talking about OT and Critical Infrastructure security recently. Make sure everything that can be remotely controlled and monitored is considered. It's no longer "just" a vending machine or refrigerator. Are you up on your environmental control systems? How about the data center? CCTV? Double check that you've got remote servicing and support, not only for the security of those devices, but also for the security of devices which are reachable from them. Have you considered the security of a device the technician "just plugs in" to do their task? An action item from the Ahold Delhaize attack: Make sure you're clear about all the impacts from an incident. Transparency trumps future damage control.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 3 of 9

      We often talk about the risks of exposed IoT devices like this, but there are few examples of catastrophic exploits like this. It appears that in this particular case, the thermostat controls were not only exposed to the internet, but also used a well-known password scheme (the current date… yes, the password changed daily). We do not know the motivations of the attackers yet, but the food supply chain has been considered a vulnerability for a long time.

      Dr. Johannes UllrichDean of Research
    • Slide 4 of 9

      While it remains unclear if the two events are connected, food and its distribution represent another critical resource, much like water, that demands heightened protection. Recent OT best practice guidance from CISA and the FBI highlights two primary defensive actions for organizations: eliminating public internet exposure and strengthening passwords and access controls. Had either of these measures been in place, this incident would not have made the headlines.

      Curtis DukesExecutive Vice President for Security Best Practices
    • Slide 5 of 9

      To paraphrase an old saying, "If you decide to poke a hole in the basket that holds all your eggs, you really, really need to watch what is coming through that hole." You can easily understand why remote alarms from freezers might justify external monitoring. This is one of the classic examples for the "data diode" approach — regular outbound reporting without any inbound connectivity, or as a minimum only with strongly authenticated logon.

      John PescatoreDirector of Emerging Security Trends
    • Slide 6 of 9

      Last Friday in NewsBites, we were discussing Cyber Informed Engineering and the importance of keeping physical processes within safe limits even when digital controls are compromised. Now attackers have reportedly manipulated refrigeration controls at hundreds of French supermarkets, spoiling enormous amounts of food. I find cyberattacks that damage the food supply particularly heinous. We rightly worry about attacks against hospitals, but food safety and availability deserve serious alarm, too. As Johannes points out, these controllers apparently had Internet exposure and a painfully predictable password scheme. Strong authentication and access restrictions matter enormously, but so do independent temperature monitoring, out-of-band alarms, local overrides, and physical safety limits that attackers cannot simply change through the compromised system. OT security isn't limited to power plants and factories. It's in the grocery store aisle, too.

      Ed SkoudisPresident
    • Slide 7 of 9

      This is extremely concerning. You might not think these devices are highly impactful, but weaponizing smart, temperature-controlled systems is a serious threat to many Western countries. You now have highly motivated attackers who are thousands of miles away spoiling food _en masse_ for the Western world. Hopefully retailers take their importance in the supply chain to heart. We have more technology today to properly isolate and control these systems at the port level with microsegmentation, or at the network level with macrosegmentation; we should enforce those controls. Will it be painful? Yes? The other painful thing is throwing out all the food in inventory.

      Moses FrostSenior Red Team Operator
    • Slide 8 of 9

      Any attack on critical infrastructure — to include where we source our food and water — is an attack on civilians. I think this also illustrates the supply chain's impact on the “kinetic world.” Intermarché, U, Leclerc, and others don't share a computer network, but they could share a refrigeration vendor or maintenance provider, and Intermarché pointed to "a service provider that manages refrigeration systems." This means that sometimes “spray and pray” attacks or unintended overflow beyond an original intended target can have widespread effects. It also reminds me of what I said about the NCSC advisory last month: Exposure is rarely a decision someone approved. More often it comes from vendor remote support that nobody owns. Ed's point about independent monitoring is borne out here, too. One employee reported that "the on-call alarm never rang," while staff who were alerted overnight were reportedly able to fix things by hand. If you run facilities with remote-managed equipment: (1) Ask your service providers how and from where they access your controllers so you can update your monitoring accordingly; (2) Push on those vendors to use secure access solutions and just-in-time access over less-safe methods like old-school VNC or RDP; and (3) Make sure you have disaster recovery and business continuity plans that include on-site manual procedures for systems typically managed remotely.

      Melissa BischopingDirector of Secure Operations and Enablement
    • Slide 9 of 9

      Using the public networks in OT is inherently risky and justifies all of the measures that my colleagues have identified and recommended. Note that a password with a life of 24 hours used across multiple enterprises and hundreds of devices, does not meet the requirements of Strong Authentication (at least two kinds of evidence, at least one of which is resistant to replay).

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 12 Oct 2026

    Patch Now: GitLab CE/EE Max-Severity Flaw

    GitLab's Critical Patch Release on October 12, 2026, released GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) 19.4.2, 19.3.4, and 19.2.8, including a fix for one maximum-severity and five high-severity flaws. CVE-2026-97229, CVSS score 10.0, allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server by using a specially crafted regular expression to exploit insufficient regular expression validation in a CI/CD configuration. GitLab credits "joaxcar" for reporting the flaw through the company's bug bounty program with HackerOne. Three high-severity flaws affect both GitLab CE and EE: a cross-site scripting issue allowing arbitrary JavaScript execution (CVE-2026-92883), an improper authorization issue allowing unauthorized execution of CI/CD pipelines (CVE-2026-16301), and a permissive regular expression issue that could cause targeted CI/CD pipelines to execute specially crafted content and could lead to exposure of protected environment variables (CVE-2026-14814). The other two high-severity flaws affect just GitLab EE: an incorrect authorization issue allowing unauthenticated arbitrary execution of a transferred project's CI/CD pipelines with the new group's privileges (CVE-2026-81839), and improper neutralization of input for LLM prompting that could cause "unintended command execution attributed to other users" in the GitLab Duo Agent Platform (CVE-2026-96893). GitLab strongly recommends users upgrade affected installations to the latest versions as soon as possible.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 5

      GitLab.com is already running the patched versions; GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. The flaw impacts all types of GitLab deployments — in other words, just update all your instances now. For security fixes, GitLab releases the details of each vulnerability publicly 90 days after the release in which they are patched.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 5

      GitLab has patched several vulnerabilities recently. This issue is particularly severe as it does not require authentication and allows for code execution.

      Dr. Johannes UllrichDean of Research
    • Slide 3 of 5

      Here we go again. How many GitLab criticals in the last few months? I'll say the same thing I always do: This system holds your source code, your pipeline config, and your secrets, so it needs to be at the top of your patch list. To be fair to GitLab, there's no report of exploitation yet. GitLab.com is already patched, and the advisory says the RCE works "under certain conditions," which they haven't spelled out.

      The bug I'd ask you to look at twice is CVE-2026-96893 in the Duo Agent Platform. It's rated lower, but an authenticated user can inject content into AI agent instructions that results in "unintended command execution attributed to other users." That last part should worry anyone doing forensics, because if the audit log says Alice ran it, but an agent did it because of something Bob planted, your investigation starts from the wrong person. As an industry we must consider that agent plugins and skills are now a patch and hygiene surface. Attribution is getting messier in this agentic attack world, and I don't see that trend going away anytime soon.

      Melissa BischopingDirector of Secure Operations and Enablement
    • Slide 4 of 5

      Yowza! This list of GitLab vulnerabilities reads like a whole set of SANS course labs: unauthenticated RCE, CI/CD authorization flaws, potential exposure of protected environment variables, and prompt injection that could cause an AI agent to execute commands attributed to other users. In a training lab, that would be a blast. On a production system that builds and deploys your software, it's a nightmare. Johannes is absolutely right to highlight the unauthenticated code execution, but the breadth of issues here deserves attention, too. CI/CD systems often hold source code, secrets, and deployment privileges reaching deep into the environment. Treat that infrastructure like the crown jewel it often is. Patch this one, folks!

      Ed SkoudisPresident
    • Slide 5 of 5

      GitLab has grown to nearly $1B in revenue in its most recent fiscal year. Hopefully this spurt of high severity flaws is the fruit of using some of the increased profit on real increases in securing their infrastructure.

      John PescatoreDirector of Emerging Security Trends

  • 08 Oct 2026

    CrowdStrike Investigation of Cyberattacks on South Korean Banks May Have Turned Up Information That Identified Hacker

    While investigating a series of AI-assisted cyberattacks targeting South Korean financial institutions, researchers at CrowdStrike "identified infrastructure associated with a targeted campaign ... that resulted in exfiltrated data." The campaign ran from late September through early October 2026. CrowdStrike writes that "the threat actor leveraged ARTEX, a recently released open-source agentic penetration testing (pentesting) tool developed in China, alongside large language models (LLMs)." CrowdStrike also discovered evidence that could help identify the individual responsible for the intrusions: AI session logs revealed a request to compose a resume which may contain details that point to the attacker. Korean officials are investigating the attacks, which have compromised personal data belonging to at least 68,000 individuals at multiple financial institutions. The compromised information includes borrowing history, incomes, phone numbers, and names.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 4

      This reinforces the observation that financially motivated threat actors are actively using AI to speed their attacks, increasing the tempo. Our defenses remain essentially the same; what has changed is our response window. You need to have a risk-based tiering of systems where most of them fall into automated updates and where security controls are implemented as SOP. This way you have resources to throw at analysis, regression testing, and planning on high-impact, riskier (to the business) systems. Don't forget to use the AI capabilities of your existing toolset. Even your CFO, who begrudgingly gives you 11:58PM to 12:01AM downtime, appreciates that you don't wish to join the list of victims, but may miss that you're trying to stack the deck in their favor to avoid future awkward conversations, so tell them so. It's easy to forget you've got the same business goals in mind. The better your relationships are with other parts of the organization, the easier it will be to talk about improvements you need and for them to talk about their business/mission requirements and come up with cool ways to achieve both.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 4

      The resume request was amusing, but the other evidence (session histories, configs, memory files) in the actor’s open directories is more interesting to me. Agentic tools generate abundant state; whoever finds the right evidence and can piece it together first wins, whether that's the attacker finding the evidence needed to pivot through your environment, or you finding the evidence of the back-and-forth and iteration on activity in real-time. Economically, open-source agents plus cheap APIs let low-skill actors launch rapid intrusions, which has already been observed widely. Barriers were low with RaaS and access brokers, but cheap and prevalent AI lowers them further. Overall, AI attacks are faster but leave far more noise and artifacts. Therefore, parsing them demands equal AI skill from investigators and leaves minutes, not hours or days, for preservation and analysis. Preserve evidence quickly and comprehensively: tmp files, network requests, timestamps, and heartbeat cadence can reveal agent “thinking” patterns that I personally find really interesting and look forward to future research on. Monitor east-west traffic as attackers use agents internally. AI attacks differ not just in speed but in artifact type and noise, requiring new sleuthing to distinguish success, noise, or deception. I’m optimistic, though. This is forcing a shift in how we think about real-time IR capabilities.

      Melissa BischopingDirector of Secure Operations and Enablement
    • Slide 3 of 4

      A resume request in an AI session log that might help identify the attacker? Ya gotta love it when attackers mess up like that. We spend plenty of time talking about how AI can amplify offensive capabilities, but poorly secured AI tooling can also leave an enormous trail of artifacts for investigators. Prompts, tool calls, session histories, and intermediate files can become a treasure trove of evidence. Kudos to CrowdStrike for finding and analyzing this material. And remember, automation can amplify attackers’ operational mistakes, too!

      Ed SkoudisPresident
    • Slide 4 of 4

      It is essential that we hold the user, not the tool, responsible.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 12 Oct 2026

    Let's Encrypt Certificate Life Cycle Change Schedule

    Open Certificate Authority (CA) Let’s Encrypt will be shortening the lifecycle of its certificates starting early next year. Currently, Let's Encrypt certificates have a 90-day lifespan. As of February 10, 2027, all certificates issued by Let’s Encrypt will expire after 64 days by default, and subscribers will have the option of choosing shorter lifespans for their certificates. Let's Encrypt writes that it "will switch to issuing 64-day certificates in [its] staging environment on October 14, 2026 to enable testing, ... [and] recommend[s] testing in staging before the change takes effect in production." The last 90-day certificate is expected to expire on May 11, 2027, and Let's Encrypt will not revoke any certificates as a part of the lifespan change process. The change to 64-day certificates is a step toward a planned certificate lifespan reduction to 45 days in 2028. Let's Encrypt also notes that the authorization reuse period will shrink from 30 days to 10 days in February 2027; in 2028, the authorization reuse period will be further reduced to seven hours.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 6

      At this point you should be using automatic processes to keep your certificates updated, making the process of keeping them updated transparent, regardless of certificate lifespan. Some of you are saying you're already using their 45 day certificates, this is not a concern; my point is that the days of manual certificate update and deployment need to be long past. Make sure that your automated renewal processes don't hard code the renewal interval — look for values like 83, 80, or 60 days — and that you have not specifically configured your ACME client to rely on validation reuse. Fix issues now; don't wait for May. They'll just get forgotten or skipped.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 6

      Certificate lifetimes will continue to shrink over the next few years. Best to get ready now and ensure proper automated renewal procedures are in place. Let's Encrypt offers a "shortlived" profile that can be used to retrieve certificates that are valid for only seven days. Try using them in a test domain to see if you can properly maintain and rotate them on time.

      Dr. Johannes UllrichDean of Research
    • Slide 3 of 6

      Let's Encrypt has been ahead of the curve in shortening certificate lifespans, which is a good thing. The certificate issuers should all focus on increasing the strength of registration/authorization in certificate issuance processes.

      John PescatoreDirector of Emerging Security Trends
    • Slide 4 of 6

      Johannes's suggestion to test with very short-lived certificates is a good one. When doing so, make sure to exercise the entire certificate lifecycle, not just renewal. Does the new certificate actually make it to every endpoint where it needs to be installed? Do services reload? Does monitoring catch failures before users do? If one step breaks, can the automation recover? Shorter certificate lifetimes can improve security, but they'll also expose brittle handoffs in our operations. A certificate that renews successfully but never gets deployed to production isn't doing you much good.

      Ed SkoudisPresident
    • Slide 5 of 6

      Expect this trend to continue across every CA as the industry addresses broken revocation mechanisms, reduces risk windows for compromised keys, and automates certificate management. In short, shorter certificate lifespans provide a guaranteed cleanup mechanism for various security risks.

      Curtis DukesExecutive Vice President for Security Best Practices
    • Slide 6 of 6

      As CAs, go the representation made by Let's Encrypt, Domain Ownership Validation, is already fairly weak. On the other hand, Let's Encrypt's leadership has encouraged the pervasive use of encryption at the transport layer.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 09 Oct 2026

    FBI Seizes Malicious Chinese Web Domains Related to Flax Typhoon

    The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has seized seven domains that support hacking tools used and operated by Chinese security firm Integrity Technology Group (Integrity Tech), which has ties to the government of the People's Republic of China (PRC). The tools have been used to scan and, in some cases, break into critical infrastructure and other networks around the world. Court documents indicate that the threat actors "created and used a network of internet-connected devices infected with a variant of Mirai malware" to conduct scans of targeted networks with one of those tools, known as Microscan. The other tool, FishHub, was allegedly used by the threat actors to "facilitate the exploitation of computer networks through spear phishing." The threat actors involved are known as Flax Typhoon. In related news, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) along with cybersecurity-related agencies in Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, Spain, and the UK, published a cybersecurity advisory last week, warning of Flax Typhoon's activity and providing technical details about the threat actors' activity. The document includes a list of CVEs the threat actors are known to have exploited, indicators of compromise (IoCs), and key actions users are advised to take.

    Editor's Notes

    The 58-page advisory lays out a lot of familiar mitigations regardless of the threat actor; this is only two pages, so you can digest this over coffee. You need to review the entire list for areas you may have missed or skipped. Make sure they are all covered; don't just say “got it” and move on. The majority of the document (38 pages of it) is the IoCs — get those to your threat hunters to see what they come up with. Some of these are older and you're only going to find them in your offline logs if at all.

    Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor

  • 12 Oct 2026

    iRhythm Breach Affects at Least 360,000 Individuals

    iRhythm, a manufacturer of cardiac monitoring devices, says that a June cybersecurity incident compromised personal information, including Protected Health Information (PHI) belonging to at least 360,000 individuals. The company has filed breach notices in several US states, including California, South Carolina, and Texas; the notices say the incident occurred in June 2026, and that the data compromise was the result of unauthorized access to third-party systems. The compromised data include patient names, patient contact information, iRhythm patient account numbers, iRhythm device serial numbers, insurance numbers, dates of service, and dates of birth. An iRhythm spokesperson told Recorded Future News that "the incident did not affect iRhythm clinical systems or medical devices and did not result in a loss of service or disruption to operations." An investigation determined that the intruders had access to the compromised system between June 3 and June 8 of this year; they gained initial access to the system via social engineering. A June 10 filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) indicates the threat actors demanded payment for not disclosing the stolen information.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 2

      Third-party system access using credentials obtained via social engineering. I'll take MFA for a $1,000 Alex. We're not going to stop social engineering; what we need to do is double down on comprehensive MFA, ideally phishing-resistant MFA to reduce its effectiveness. Don't forget to include training on not providing MFA tokens/codes to ANYONE. The idea of phishing-resistant MFA is there are no codes or other shareable components, avoiding this scenario.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 2

      While one now recommends the use of strong authentication in all multi-user systems, the failure to use it on enterprise Internet facing applications is reckless.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 12 Oct 2026

    FBI Arrests Cyber Exec on Suspicion of ShinyHunters Conspiracy

    Following a threat actor's defacement of FBIjobs[.]gov, the claimed theft of FBI agents' sensitive personal information, and the bureau's termination of a third-party contractor whose unpatched system may have allowed the breach, FBI Director Kash Patel announced on social media on October 9 that "another suspected co-conspirator" had been arrested. While the announcement does not give additional details, Brian Krebs uncovered information indicating that the individual arrested was 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive with ties to Cypfer and CyberSteward, Canadian cybersecurity firms that specialize in cyber risk consultation, incident response, and ransomware recovery. Krebs cites indexed court records and sources close to the matter to show that Dubrovsky appears to have been arrested on October 8 while attending the NetDiligence Cyber Risk Summit in Philadelphia, PA, on charges of “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” before the case was transferred to the Eastern District of Texas, which Krebs's sources allege is "the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation." Dubrovsky announced the publication of his book, "Cyber Extortion Strategic Response," on October 4, whose stated thesis is that "communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay. Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move."

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 4

      Two weeks ago I wrote about ShinyHunters' threats against the FBI, and how much cybercrime has come to resemble legitimate business. I didn't expect the next chapter to involve someone from the legitimate business side. While the facts are sealed and murky, the story raises a question the industry should ask regardless of how this case ends. When you bring in a ransomware negotiator, you hand them your most sensitive facts on your worst day. That's an extraordinary level of trust, and most organizations extend it through an insurance panel list or an IR retainer, sometimes without deeply vetting how that firm vets its own people. Krebs reports that his sources expect charges against principals at other negotiation firms "may be forthcoming." If that turns out to be true, it'll be a hard year for a profession that, in my experience, is mostly made up of responsible people doing difficult work in good faith. So before your next incident, consider these practical steps: (1) Ask your IR and negotiation providers how they screen staff and control access to case data; (2) Find out who on their side can see your financial position and ransom deliberations; (3) Make sure engagement with criminals is a sanctioned, supervised function on your own team too, not something one person handles alone.

      Melissa BischopingDirector of Secure Operations and Enablement
    • Slide 2 of 4

      Anybody else recalling last year's incident at DigitalMint? Ransomware remains lucrative, which is why it's still going strong, and the temptations are a sufficient lure to cause one to change roles. If you're hiring such a negotiator, regrettably many private companies do pay the ransom, and you're going to want to carefully verify they are reliable. On the other side, this emphasizes the need for ongoing reliability checks. In my background, we had positions which required human reliability checks, regular screening/testing, and required codes of conduct, to conduct certain roles. These are up-front requirements, in positions where temptation to cross the line is significant. Temptation is real, and people make bad choices. Do what you can to detect and deter these actions.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 3 of 4

      This is an interesting development. Although details remain limited beyond what KrebsOnSecurity reported, previous cases have shown ransomware negotiators becoming complicit in cybercriminal activity. The cited book reference suggests that negotiators frequently build rapport with attackers — a dynamic that can sometimes be a telling indicator of deeper involvement.

      Curtis DukesExecutive Vice President for Security Best Practices
    • Slide 4 of 4

      One may infer from the title of his book that he knew what he was doing.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 09 Oct 2026

    Qilin Suspect Extradited to Germany from Japan

    A 28-year-old Russian man arrested in Japan on suspicion of involvement with an attack by the Qilin ransomware gang against a German company has now been extradited to Germany. In May 2026, the cyber special investigation department of the Japanese National Police Agency (NPA) collaborated in an investigation with police departments in Tokyo, Osaka, and Kyoto to initially determine the suspect's whereabouts after learning of his plan to visit Japan as a tourist. The suspect was detained in Osaka under a German arrest warrant, and has now officially been turned over to German authorities under Japanese extradition law, according to a press release from NPA. Qilin is believed to have carried out disruptive attacks on large organizations such as Nissan, Asahi, Kuala Lumpur International Airport, Lee Enterprises, Australia's Court Services Victoria, the US city of Sugar Land in Texas, and the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.

    Editor's Notes

    Given Qilin’s alleged attacks on Japanese companies, I'm surprised the suspect was not kept in Japan. Kudos to German Law Enforcement! The Qilin ransomware gang attracted law enforcement's attention in 2024, and was one of the most active ransomware gangs in 2025. This continues the trend of successfully arresting members of ransomware gangs, hopefully changing the risk-reward equation in that industry. Even so, given the financial scope of ransomware, it's not clear there will be a lot of change quickly, so we need to continue to be diligent, resilient, and vigilant.

    Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor

  • 10 Oct 2026

    Judge Imposes 32-Month Sentence on Former Employee for Extortion and Damaging Protected Computer

    A US District Judge in New Jersey has sentenced Daniel Rhyne to 32 months in prison for intentionally damaging his former employer's IT networks and attempting to extort his co-workers by threatening to shut down servers. Rhyne was employed "as a core infrastructure engineer at a U.S.-based industrial company headquartered in New Jersey." Court documents indicate that between November 8 and November 25, 2023, Rhyne remotely accessed his employer's network without authorization using an administrative account and deleted domain admin accounts, changed passwords for multiple domain user and admin accounts, and effectively blocked access to hundreds of servers and thousands of workstations. In April 2026, Rhyne pleaded guilty to charges of extortion in relation to a threat to cause damage to a protected computer and intentional damage to a protected computer.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 3

      The investigation highlights the value of collecting logs for analysis. Remember to investigate options like a data lake for offline log storage over longer intervals. This guy started setting things up in 2023 before pulling the trigger in 2025. Now that you have comprehensive logs, are you catching the right things? For example, could you have triggered an alert at the deletion of Domain Administrator accounts or broad scale password changes? How about detecting unauthorized changes or sessions? New tools make this analysis easier; it's worth pulling this thread as well.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 3

      Justice served. CISOs ought to leverage this outcome as a real-world case study in their annual cybersecurity training programs.

      Curtis DukesExecutive Vice President for Security Best Practices
    • Slide 3 of 3

      The lesson for the rest of us is that, when terminating an employee, it is as essential to terminate all privileges and authorities, as it is to remove them from the payroll.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

Internet Storm Center Tech Corner

SANS Internet Storm Center StormCast Tuesday, October 13, 2026

Integer Overflow Issue Impacts GitLab CE/EE; Let’s Encrypt 64-Day Certificates; Midnight Mimosa Pre-Installed Android Malware; Progress MarkLogic Patches

In today's episode: a critical GitLab integer overflow that allows unauthenticated code execution, Let’s Encrypt moving to 64-day TLS certificates in February 2027, Midnight Mimosa malware pre-installed on cheap Android phones, and Progress MarkLogic security updates.

https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10134

CVE-2026-97229 - Integer Overflow Issue in CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler Impacts GitLab CE/EE

An integer overflow in GitLab's CI/CD regular expression compiler lets unauthenticated users execute arbitrary code on self-managed GitLab servers. It was reported responsibly through HackerOne, and no public exploit is known yet. Patch on-premises installations quickly.

https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-4-2-released/#cve-2026-97229---integer-overflow-issue-in-cicd-regular-expression-compiler-impacts-gitlab-ceee

Let’s Encrypt 64-Day Certificate Lifetimes Coming Feb 2027

Let’s Encrypt staging certificates drop to 64 days on October 14th, and all new production certificates follow on February 10th, 2027. Test your automation now, and adjust certificate expiration alerts for shorter-lived certificates.

https://letsencrypt.org/2026/10/07/64-day-certs.html

Midnight Mimosa: Malware Pre-Installed on Android Phones

Bitdefender found Midnight Mimosa malware pre-installed on cheap Android phones sold under flagship-like names such as S25 Ultra and i17 Pro. The malware disables the Google Play Store to evade detection and supports clickjacking, a proxy botnet, and ad fraud.

https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/midnight-mimosa-malware

Progress MarkLogic Critical Security Alert Bulletin – October 2026

Progress released October 2026 updates for the MarkLogic data management platform and NoSQL database, with some vulnerabilities rated CVSS 9.9. The most severe let users with low-level query privileges execute arbitrary code, partly through a legacy API that is still enabled.

https://community.progress.com/s/article/Marklogic-Critical-Security-Alert-Bulletin-October-2026

SANS Internet Storm Center StormCast Monday, October 12, 2026

TLP Overuse; AgentCorruption SSRF in Amazon Bedrock Agents; Palo Alto GlobalProtect VPN Exploited by Ransomware (CVE-2026-0257)

In today's episode: why the Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) should not replace internal data classification, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw in Amazon Bedrock AI agents that exposed credentials through the EC2 instance metadata service (IMDS), and ransomware groups exploiting a Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect authentication bypass.

https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10132

Why TLP Should Not Replace Your Internal Information Classification

The Traffic Light Protocol from FIRST defines who threat intelligence may be shared with, from TLP:CLEAR to TLP:RED, but not how to protect it in transit. Organizations still need their own classification and safeguards, such as encryption, instead of sending TLP:AMBER data in plain email.

https://isc.sans.edu/diary/Why+TLP+should+not+replace+your+internal+information+classification/33414

AgentCorruption: How A Single Prompt Collapsed The Entire Cloud Security Model

Zenity Labs found a now-fixed server-side request forgery vulnerability in Amazon Bedrock AI agents. A prompt could make an agent fetch and reveal credentials from the EC2 instance metadata service, made possible by IMDSv1 and overly broad permissions. Restrict the URLs your AI agents can reach and always use IMDSv2.

https://labs.zenity.io/post/agentcorruption-how-a-single-prompt-collapsed-the-entire-cloud-security-model

Palo Alto GlobalProtect VPN Vulnerability Exploited by Ransomware (CVE-2026-0257)

ReliaQuest reports ransomware actors exploiting an authentication bypass in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS GlobalProtect and Prisma Access to open unauthorized VPN sessions. Patch VPN gateways, and keep VPN clients updated too.

https://x.com/ReliaQuestTR/status/2108647641240465707

https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2026-0257
